content: The uterus, also known as the womb, is the primary reproductive organ in females of most mammalian species, including humans. It is a hollow, muscular organ located in the pelvis. One end of the uterus, the cervix, opens into the vagina, while the other end is connected to the fallopian tubes on both sides. The term uterus is commonly used in medical and professional contexts, whereas womb is more frequently used in everyday language. The plural form of uterus is uteri. The primary function of the uterus is to receive a fertilized ovum, which implants into the endometrium (the inner lining of the uterus). The endometrium provides nourishment to the developing embryo through specialized blood vessels. The fertilized ovum develops into an embryo, then a fetus, and remains in the uterus until childbirth. During pregnancy, the uterus expands significantly, partially extending into the abdominal cavity due to anatomical constraints such as the pelvis. In mammals, the uterus exists in four main forms, depending on the species. In humans, the uterus is situated within the pelvis, positioned dorsally (and slightly rostrally) to the urinary bladder and ventrally to the rectum. Outside of pregnancy, the uterus in humans measures only a few centimeters in diameter. The pathway to the uterus, from the external to the internal structures, includes the vulva, vagina, cervix (with its external and internal orifices), and the corpus uteri (the body of the uterus). The uppermost part of the uterus is called the fundus. The uterus is composed of several layers, arranged from the innermost to the outermost. The uterus is primarily supported by the pelvic diaphragm and the urogenital diaphragm. Ligaments such as the broad ligament, round ligament, suspensory ligament of the ovary, and infundibulopelvic ligament do not play a direct role in uterine support. Under normal conditions, the uterus is both anteflexed (bent forward) and anteverted (tilted forward). These terms describe its typical anatomical position. During early fetal development, the bilateral Müllerian ducts form. In males, these ducts regress due to the secretion of Müllerian-inhibiting factor (MIF) from the testes. In females, the Müllerian ducts develop into the fallopian tubes and the uterus. In humans, the lower segments of the two ducts fuse to form a single uterus. However, in cases of uterine malformations, this fusion process may be disrupted. The various uterine forms observed in different mammalian species result from varying degrees of fusion of the Müllerian ducts. Pathological conditions affecting the uterus include: Uterine prolapse Cervical carcinoma (malignant neoplasm of the cervix) Uterine carcinoma (malignant neoplasm of the uterus) Ectopic pregnancy Uterine fibroids (benign neoplasms) Adenomyosis (ectopic growth of endometrial tissue within the myometrium) Pyometra (infection leading to pus accumulation in the uterus) Uterine malformations Uterine didelphys (a condition where the uterus and/or vagina are split or doubled) Retroverted uterus (a uterus tilted backward) Rokitansky syndrome (a congenital absence or underdevelopment of the uterus and upper vagina) Myoma (benign tumors of the uterine muscle) Additional imaging studies, such as CT scans, are sometimes used to evaluate the uterus, particularly in cases of pregnancy or suspected pathology. For example, CT imaging may be employed in pregnant patients when the benefits of the scan outweigh the associated risks. These images can provide detailed views of the gravid uterus and its surrounding structures. Other anatomical illustrations and models, such as sagittal sections of the female pelvis or depictions of uterine blood vessels, are also used to study the uterus and its associated anatomy.
